title: Sysmon: The SOC Analyst's Best Friend
description: Advanced Windows logging with Sysmon for deep visibility.

slides.title: Sysmon: The Upgrade You Need 🚀
slides.content:
# System Monitor (Sysmon)

**Sysmon** is a free tool from Microsoft's Sysinternals suite. Once installed, it becomes a **driver** that monitors the system at the kernel level and writes detailed events to the **Windows Event Log** (`Applications and Services Logs/Microsoft/Windows/Sysmon/Operational`).

**Why is Sysmon better than standard Windows Logging?**

| Feature | Windows Default | Sysmon |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Process Creation | Event ID 4688 (Limited) | Event ID 1 (Hashes, Parent info, GUID) |
| Network Connections | Limited to Firewall | Event ID 3 (Links Process to IP) |
| File Creation | Not logged by default | Event ID 11 (FileCreate) |
| Registry Changes | Not logged by default | Event ID 13 (Registry Value Set) |
| Process Injection | **Impossible to see** | Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) |

slides.title: Sysmon Event ID 1: The Ultimate Process Log
slides.content: This is the most important Sysmon event. It gives you a SHA256 hash of the executable.
slides.codeSnippet:
EventID: 1 (Process Create)
Image: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
CommandLine: cmd.exe /c whoami
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE
ParentCommandLine: "C:\Program Files...\WINWORD.EXE" /n "C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\malicious.docm"
Hashes: SHA256=ABC123...

# See the difference? We now know WORD spawned CMD. We have the exact document name. We have the hash to check on VirusTotal.

quizData.question: Which Sysmon Event ID specifically logs when a process tries to inject code into another process (a technique used for credential theft)?
quizData.explanation: Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) is the definitive event for detecting process injection.

slides.title: Sysmon Event ID 3: Network Connections 🔌
slides.content:
# Linking Processes to IPs

Standard Windows logs don't easily tell you **which process** made a specific outbound connection. Sysmon Event ID 3 does.

**Field:** `Image` (The process that made the connection).
**Field:** `DestinationIp`.
**Field:** `DestinationPort`.

**Use Case:**
1.  Firewall alert: `192.168.1.101` connected to malicious IP `185.142.53.21`.
2.  Query Sysmon Event ID 3 for `DestinationIp=185.142.53.21`.
3.  Result: `Image: C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Local\Temp\dropper.exe`.

**Now you know exactly which file caused the alert!**

slides.title: Sysmon Configuration ⚙️
slides.content:
## It's Only as Good as the Config

Sysmon is a sensor. It doesn't alert by itself. You need a **configuration file** (XML) that tells it what to look for and what to ignore (exclude).

**Popular Community Configs:**
*   **SwiftOnSecurity Sysmon Config:** The industry standard starter config. It filters out noise and highlights suspicious events.
*   **Olaf Hartong Sysmon-Modular:** Advanced, granular configuration.

**Pro Tip:** A poorly configured Sysmon that logs **everything** will fill your SIEM storage and cost you a fortune. **Exclusions are just as important as inclusions.**
